rationale: Although framed around multiple uses of an irrigation common-pool system, this empirical socio-legal case study is directly relevant to household and community domestic water service access (thus not excluded under Exclusion Criterion 7). Based on a stratified survey of 156 households, direct standpipe observations, focus groups, and key informant interviews in Kirindi Oya, Sri Lanka, the paper examines rule-type mechanisms directly governing domestic piped water access—including NWS&DB permitted-use rules, monthly user charges (Rs 11), collective enforcement via disconnection and a Rs 250 reconnection fee, informal community accommodation at standposts, drought allocation priority rules, and institutional membership rules excluding non-irrigators, women, and domestic water agencies from allocation bodies—and reports qualitative empirical findings on source reliance, de facto access, and low standpipe supply reliability.
